abstracts.abstract: This letter introduces a novel theoretical framework for sparse signal recovery that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between measurement matrices and sparse priors. Unlike conventional compressed sensing approaches that treat measurement design and sparse reconstruction as separate optimization problems, we propose a unified framework where the sensing operator and sparse representation are jointly optimized within a single bi-level optimization paradigm. The key insight is that the restricted isometry property can be relaxed by exploiting the statistical structure of the sparse coefficient distribution, enabling recovery guarantees under substantially weaker conditions. We derive novel concentration inequalities that characterize the sample complexity required for exact recovery with arbitrary sparse priors. Furthermore, we prove that the proposed framework achieves order-optimal sampling rates that scale logarithmically with the signal dimension, regardless of the sparsity level. The theoretical analysis reveals an interesting connection between information-theoretic limits and algorithmic stability in sparse recovery. Extensive numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world signals validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins in both recovery accuracy and computational efficiency.

This letter presents an improved theoretical analysis of adaptive filtering algorithms under non-stationary environments. While the conventional least mean square (LMS) algorithm has been extensively studied under the independent assumption between input and weight vectors, this assumption rarely holds in practical applications. We develop a tighter mean-square error (MSE) bound by incorporating the statistical coupling between the input vector and the weight error vector through a novel correlation factor. The key contribution lies in deriving explicit expressions for the transient and steady-state MSE that account for the time-varying autocorrelation of the input signal. We prove that the proposed bound is always tighter than existing bounds and reduces to the conventional result when the correlation factor approaches unity. Additionally, we establish sufficient conditions for mean-square convergence that are less restrictive than those previously reported in the literature. The theoretical analysis provides new insights into the impact of input signal statistics on adaptive filter performance and offers a systematic approach for selecting step-size parameters in practical implementations. Simulation results confirm the accuracy of the derived expressions across various non-stationary scenarios.

This letter proposes a novel neural-augmented array processing system that fundamentally transforms the way acoustic signals are captured and beamformed in reverberant environments. The proposed architecture replaces traditional delay-and-sum beamformers with a learnable neural network module that operates directly on raw microphone array signals. Unlike conventional approaches that require explicit acoustic transfer function modeling and manual parameter tuning, the neural-augmented system automatically learns optimal spatial filtering strategies from training data. The core innovation lies in the design of a physics-informed neural network that incorporates fundamental acoustic wave propagation constraints as differentiable operators, ensuring physically meaningful beamforming patterns while retaining the flexibility of data-driven learning. The system employs a hierarchical attention mechanism that dynamically weights frequency bands based on their signal-to-noise ratio contributions. Real-time processing is achieved through a lightweight model architecture that maintains low latency suitable for live audio applications. Experiments conducted in challenging acoustic environments demonstrate that the proposed system achieves substantial improvements in speech intelligibility and noise reduction compared to conventional beamforming methods, particularly in scenarios with multiple concurrent talkers and significant room reverberation.

This letter presents an enhanced biomedical signal processing pipeline for real-time seizure detection from long-term electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings. The proposed system comprises three novel components: a compact convolutional neural network feature extractor optimized for edge deployment, an adaptive threshold mechanism that accounts for inter-patient variability, and a lightweight temporal modeling module that captures seizure onset dynamics. The feature extractor employs depthwise separable convolutions with dilated temporal kernels to achieve a 78% reduction in model parameters compared to existing approaches while maintaining comparable detection accuracy. A key improvement is the introduction of a personalized calibration scheme that adapts the decision threshold based on the patient's baseline EEG characteristics, significantly reducing false alarm rates. The temporal modeling module utilizes a recurrent architecture with selective memory mechanisms that prioritize recent input while retaining relevant historical context. The complete system operates with a latency of less than 250 milliseconds on embedded hardware platforms, making it suitable for closed-loop therapeutic interventions. Evaluations on a large multi-center dataset comprising 1,200 patients demonstrate that the proposed system achieves 94.3% sensitivity with 0.12 false alarms per hour, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins.
